For any positive x, y, the algorithm has a fundamental problem: the loop condition `b == (x*q + y*s)` checks an invariant that the algorithm maintains exactly. Since the invariant always holds (in exact arithmetic), the loop never terminates naturally. When the algorithm reaches `b = 0` (which it always does — the subtractive GCD reduces b to 0), the loop continues with `a > b` (since a = gcd ≥ 1), executing `a = a - 0` (unchanged) while `p = p - q` and `r = r - s` grow without bound. The Bézout coefficients q and s are nonzero at this point (s starts at 1 and is modified during the algorithm), so p and r grow linearly until `p - q` or `r - s` overflows.

Even during the algorithm itself, the products `x * q` and `y * s` in the loop condition can overflow for large inputs (e.g., x = 2000000000, y = 1073741824 causes `y * s` to overflow when s reaches 2).

So every positive (x, y) pair eventually produces signed integer overflow. The safe region is exactly {x ≤ 0 or y ≤ 0}, an L-shape. The largest rectangular box inside it is a half-strip: restrict one parameter to non-positive values and leave the other at full range, keeping ~50% of the declared domain.
